item.title: Investigation of the timing performance of double-sided $p$-type 3D silicon sensors produced by CNM
item.description: arXiv:2611.13642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the timing performance and spatial uniformity of double-sided $p$-type 3D silicon sensors produced by the Centro Nacional de Microelectr\'onica (CNM). Three sensor layouts are studied: hexagonal and square geometries with an inter-electrode spacing of \SI{30}{\micro\meter}, and a hexagonal geometry with an inter-electrode spacing of \SI{50}{\micro\meter}. The sensors are characterized using a \SI{1064}{\nano\meter} infrared laser and a custom two-stage wide-band readout. Measurements with a $^{90}$Sr source are used to establish a minimum-ionizing-particle-like reference for the laser signal. The timing resolution improves with increasing bias voltage for all three layouts. Two-dimensional laser scans are used to study the position dependence of the timing response and to quantify its uniformity. Among the investigated devices, the square \SI{30}{\micro\meter} geometry shows the best overall timing performance at the highest measured bias voltage.
item.dc:creator: C. Liao, C. Betancourt, M. Togawa, D. Bortoletto, N. Moffat, G. Pellegrini

item.title: SiPM optical readout of a PICOSEC Micromegas precise timing detector
item.description: arXiv:2611.13830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By combining a Cherenkov radiator with a semi-transparent photocathode and a two-stage Micromegas amplification element, PICOSEC Micromegas detectors have achieved <20 ps charged-particle time resolution with electronic readout of induced signals. Building upon this performance, we describe SiPM-based optical readout as a novel technique for PICOSEC Micromegas detectors. Single-channel detector prototypes based on glass Micromegas technology were read out with an array of SiPMs. To allow operation in a strongly quenched gas mixture, a solid wavelength shifter is integrated in the glass Micromegas to convert UV scintillation to the visible range and maximise scintillation light output. Timing performance of glass Micromegas in electronic and optical readout modes is compared and <150 ps time resolution is achieved by optically read out scintillation light signals. The achievable spatial resolution from centre-of-gravity reconstruction of event positions from the amplitudes of signals on multiple SiPM channels is {\sigma} = 1.25 mm. This demonstrates the possibility of dual-readout of PICOSEC glass Micromegas: electronic signals and optical signals. Finally, camera-based optical readout is presented to demonstrate imaging as another avenue for position reconstruction.

item.title: Characterization of BNLs 20 and 30 micrometer thick LGADs for the Electron Ion Collider
item.description: arXiv:2611.14040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The 20 and 30 micrometer thick Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) produced at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) were evaluated. Detailed electrical measurements indicate well-formed and stable gain layers with consistently low leakage currents. Transient Current Technique (TCT) was used to evaluate the gain. Fast-laser timing studies demonstrate time resolutions at the level of a few tens of picoseconds. To assess operational longevity under realistic conditions for Electron-Ion Collider sub-detector systems, devices were irradiated with 30 MeV and 60 MeV protons to fluences of 10^13 to 10^14 neq/cm^2, enabling a focused study of radiation-induced effects on gain stability and timing performance.

item.title: Optical characterization of microcellular PET and crystallized PEN reflectors in liquid argon for LEGEND-1000
item.description: arXiv:2611.14202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient collection of liquid argon (LAr) scintillation light is essential for background rejection in the LEGEND experiment. We investigate microcellular polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and crystallized polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) as candidate reflector materials for LEGEND-1000. Their optical responses to 450 nm light and 128 nm LAr scintillation are measured in LAr and complemented by room-temperature reflectance measurements in air. Under scintillation illumination, PET coupled to a PEN foil and crystallized PEN increase the detected photoelectron yield by factors of $2.36\pm0.11$ and $1.75\pm0.10$, respectively, relative to a black-metal-velvet reference. A Geant4-based optical model yields reflectivity estimates at $450~\mathrm{nm}$ in LAr of $(90\pm4)\%$ for PET and $(81\pm5)\%$ for crystallized PEN, compared with $(80\pm5)\%$ for the Tetratex reference. These results motivate further investigation of both materials for LAr instrumentation, including their radiopurity, long-term cryogenic stability, and performance under matched detector conditions.
item.dc:creator: Marta Babicz, Laura Baudis, Andreas Leonhardt, Francesco Piastra, Lorenzo Pietropaoli, Stefan Sch\"onert, Gloria Senatore, Esteban Tapia Pe\~nas, Tim van de Vendel

item.title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples
item.description: arXiv:2611.14447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.

item.title: Development of a Long-Term Stable Three-Axis Single-Beam Vector Optically Pumped Magnetometer Using a Buffer-Gas-Free Rubidium Vapor Cell and Direct Absorption Frequency Locking for Unshielded Geomagnetic Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.12905v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) achieve ultra-high sensitivity, yet sustaining long-term stability in unshielded, dynamic geomagnetic environments remains challenging. Here, we present the design and unshielded validation of a three-axis vector OPM achieving sub-nanotesla accuracy using an off-the-shelf rubidium (Rb) ampoule and a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL). Unlike conventional sensors, this system operates without high-pressure buffer gases, mitigating wall-collision relaxation via a single-beam geometry combined with active zero-field nulling and adiabatic 70 kHz AC heating. To suppress VCSEL thermal wavelength drift without sub-Doppler optics, active frequency stabilization based on direct absorption spectroscopy (DAS) was implemented across a wide capture range. Continuous evaluation in an unshielded laboratory in Okayama against synthetic geomagnetic records from the Kakioka and Kanoya observatories demonstrated exceptional horizontal tracking fidelity. Concurrently, the vertical transfer matrix resolved the regional geomagnetic coast effect, extracting Parkinson induction vectors reflecting regional conductivity contrast, with high robustness against DC electric railway interference. Spectral characterization showed an intrinsic white noise floor of 10-20 pT above 1 Hz, enhanced by digital oversampling beyond the 12-bit DAC quantization limit, while residual overlapped Allan deviation revealed a 0.1 nT bias instability at 100-200 s integration times. These results prove that a compact, low-cost OPM platform based on commercial components can suppress long-term drift and serve as a reliable instrument for geophysical surveys and unshielded magnetic sensing.
item.dc:creator: Minaru Kawamura

item.title: Development of a versatile modular system to study the ablation and plume expansion in a thin film
item.description: arXiv:2611.13570v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time-resolved investigation of laser ablation of thin films requires stable, repeatable, and efficient experimental environment. Conventional approaches often rely on multiple laser-ablation shots acquired at different delay times to reconstruct the temporal evolution of the process, thereby assuming shot-to-shot reproducibility. This work presents a novel modular experimental setup that addresses these challenges and enables a systematic pump--probe study of laser--matter interaction. The setup provides reliable single-pulse measurements with controlled sample positioning inside the high vacuum chamber, as well as integrated data recording, which improves redundancy and ease with which experiments can be performed. Further, the setup serves as an advanced diagnostic tool for investigating the time evolution of laser--matter interactions, ablation dynamics and laser-produced plasmas in a single laser shot, in various configurations with a temporal resolution better than 15 ns. Using this capability, we show that for a fixed ablation geometry, the transient reflectivity and transmission response depends strongly on the probing side, indicating that probing direction is an independent diagnostic variable whose omission can lead to incomplete or misleading picture of the ablation dynamics. This experimental technique can advance the understanding of surface modification and plume expansion, which are relevant to fundamental studies and also for range of applications, including laser cleaning of tokamak viewports and mirrors, pulsed laser deposition (PLD), surface structuring and laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT), among others. The present setup is versatile enough to perform these studies under different ablation configurations without implementing major changes in the experimental configuration.
item.dc:creator: Renjith Kumar R, Pabitra Kumar Mishra, B R Geethika, Hem C Joshi, Jinto Thomas

item.title: Characterization of CRYO ASIC for charge readout in the nEXO experiment
item.description: arXiv:2512.11116v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: nEXO is a proposed next-generation experiment searching for the neutrinoless double beta decay of $^{136}$Xe using a tonne-scale liquid xenon (LXe) time projection chamber (TPC). To image the ionization signals from events in the liquid xenon, the detector will employ metallized fused-silica charge collection tiles instrumented with cryogenic application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), referred to as CRYO ASIC, which are designed to operate directly in LXe to minimize input capacitance and pick-up noise. Here we present the performance of the CRYO ASIC mounted on an auxiliary printed circuit board and evaluated both in a cryogenic environmental chamber and in a dedicated LXe test stand. We demonstrate that the ASICs achieve the desired performance at liquid xenon temperatures, showing a gain stability better than 0.2% over 24-hour operation and reliable in-situ calibration using an on-chip pulser. In the LXe test stand, we show that boiling caused by the chip heat dissipation can be mitigated by operating the system above ~0.1 MPa. The in-LXe noise measured agrees with simulation, which indicates it the $150~e^-$ design requirement can be satisfied. These results establish CRYO ASIC as a viable low-noise in-LXe charge readout solution for nEXO.

item.title: Optical characterization and ionizing-radiation response of the BCF-20XL scintillating fiber
item.description: arXiv:2608.21397v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report optical characterization and ionizing-radiation measurements of the BCF-20XL scintillating fiber from Luxium Solutions, which also wavelength-shifts externally incident blue light (referred to here as Sci-WLS). Attenuation lengths were obtained from transmitted emission spectra using a 3.0 m fiber with a spectrophotometer and described with a two-component attenuation model, yielding a long attenuation length of 6.70 m and a short attenuation length of 0.16 m. The spectral measurements also reveal wavelength-dependent attenuation, with the long component increasing with wavelength and the short component becoming less significant at longer wavelengths. The scintillation response was also characterized under radioactive alpha, beta, and gamma irradiation using SiPM-based readout, providing a benchmark of the detected photoelectron response of BCF-20XL.

item.title: Reconstructing High-Fidelity Light Yield Maps for Surface LArTPCs Using Crossing Cosmic Muons
item.description: arXiv:2608.21581v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photon detection systems in liquid argon time projection chambers provide prompt scintillation light information that can improve triggering, timing, calorimetry, and interaction reconstruction. These applications require an understanding of the spatial dependence of the detected light yield (LY), which is not adequately described by a single detector-wide average. We present a method for reconstructing voxelized 3D light yield maps in surface LArTPCs using crossing cosmic muons. For each selected muon, the path length through every crossed voxel is converted to deposited energy using a minimum ionizing particle approximation, producing a linear system relating the unknown voxel light yields to the total detected photon signal. The resulting inverse problem is solved using nonnegative least squares, with an additional $L_2$ smoothness penalty used to stabilize weakly constrained voxel values. The method is studied in simulation using the ProtoDUNE-VD detector geometry and photon detection system. Reconstructed maps recover the dominant spatial structure of a visibility-based truth reference and respond as expected to changes in the photon detector configuration. Smoothness regularization reduces zero-valued voxels and localized fluctuations while leaving the detector-average light yield approximately unchanged at the selected regularization strengths. The voxel-wise RMSE relative to the truth reference is reduced by approximately 44% for the regularized reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Alex Heindel, Wei Shi, Angelo Ralaikoto, Shuaixiang Zhang, Laura Paulucci, Franciole Marinho, Maressa Pimenta Sampaio, Sanskar Jain

item.title: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) Antarctic Balloon Payload
item.description: arXiv:2604.19830v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic stratospheric balloon mission designed to provide unmatched sensitivity to low-energy (< 0.25 GeV/n) cosmic-ray antiprotons, antideuterons, and antihelium nuclei as signatures of dark matter. The distinctive GAPS particle identification technique relies on measuring the energy loss along the track of an incoming antinucleus as it slows down and is captured into an exotic atom, and then detecting the de-excitation X-rays and the nuclear annihilation products. This measurement is realized using a Tracker composed of more than 1000 custom silicon strip detectors and a plastic scintillator time-of-flight (TOF) system instrumenting more than 40 m$^2$. Together, these subsystems provide the velocity and energy resolution, stopping power, particle tracking, and X-ray identification necessary to distinguish rare antinucleus signals from the abundant positive-nucleus backgrounds, all within the constraints of a high-altitude mission. A multi-loop capillary heat pipe system has been developed to maintain the tracker operating temperature with significant mass and power savings over a conventional pump-based system. The first GAPS science payload flew for 25 days during the 2025/26 NASA Antarctic balloon campaign. We detail the design, integration, and commissioning of the payload prior to flight.
